```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.asp = 0.618
)

library(esqlabsR)
```

Clear, consistent figures are a core part of model diagnostics and of any report. This article shows how to turn scenario results into figures with `{esqlabsR}`:

- build the figures a project already defines
- create your own figures and add observed data to them
- plot a population
- apply the ESQlabs house style
- export a figure to a file
- work with the data behind a figure, such as the residuals

Every figure below uses the example project bundled with the package and the results of two of its scenarios.

Three building blocks recur below. A **DataCombined** says which simulated curves and which observed data belong together. A **Plot** describes one chart drawn from a DataCombined. A **Plot Grid** arranges Plots into one figure. All three are stored as definitions in the project. `vignette("about-the-plotting-model")` explains the structure in detail, and `vignette("reference-definition-fields")` lists the fields of each.

## Load the example and run its scenarios

Every figure in this article is built from scenario results. Work on a copy of the example, so the figures you add later do not change the installed package. `initProject()` copies the example to a temporary folder. Load the copy and run two of its scenarios: the individual scenario `aciclovir_iv` and the population scenario `aciclovir_iv_population`.

```{r setup-run}
project_dir <- withr::local_tempdir()
initProject(destination = project_dir, type = "example", createExcel = TRUE)
project <- loadProject(file.path(project_dir, "Project.json"))

scenarioResults <- runScenarios(
  project,
  scenarios = c("aciclovir_iv", "aciclovir_iv_population")
)

names(scenarioResults)
```

`scenarioResults` is a list named by scenario id. Pass it to every plotting function below. A figure can only draw scenarios that are in this list, so run every scenario a figure needs before you build it.

## Inspect the figures a project defines

Each of the three building blocks has its own section under `project$definitions`: `dataCombined`, `plots`, and `plotGrids`. Print a section to see the ids it holds, and pick out one definition by its id. Start with the Plot Grids, the figures `createPlots()` builds by default:

```{r inspect-grids}
project$definitions$plotGrids
project$definitions$plotGrids[["individual_diagnostics"]]
```

The grid `individual_diagnostics` holds one Plot, `p1`. Print that Plot to see its type and the DataCombined it draws from:

```{r inspect-plot}
project$definitions$plots[["p1"]]
```

Printing a Plot shows only four items. Its other settings, such as the time unit or the axis limits, are fields of the Plot. `names()` lists the fields that are set, and `$` reads one of them:

```{r inspect-plot-fields}
names(project$definitions$plots[["p1"]])
project$definitions$plots[["p1"]]$xUnit
```

A setting that is not in this list takes the ESQlabs default value (see [Apply the ESQlabs house style](#apply-the-esqlabs-house-style)) or the default of the plotting function.

`p1` draws from the DataCombined `aciclovir_individual`. Printing a DataCombined shows how many simulated and observed curves it holds.

```{r inspect-datacombined}
project$definitions$dataCombined[["aciclovir_individual"]]
# Inspect the simulated curve definition
project$definitions$dataCombined[["aciclovir_individual"]]$simulated[[1]]
```

A field shown as `NULL` is not set. The observed curves are under `$observed` in the same way. This curve comes from the scenario `aciclovir_iv`, so `scenarioResults` must hold that scenario for the figure to be built. `vignette("reference-definition-fields")` explains every field of the three definitions.

## Generate a project's predefined plots

`createPlots()` reads the definitions above and builds the figures. It fills each DataCombined with the simulated curves from `scenarioResults` and with the observed data the project declares.

```{r create-plots}
plotGrids <- createPlots(project, scenarioResults = scenarioResults)
```

Despite its name, `createPlots()` returns Plot Grids, not single Plots: the returned list is named after the project's Plot Grids.

```{r show-predefined}
plotGrids$individual_diagnostics
```

To build only some of the project's grids, pass their names to `plotGrids`.

```{r create-plots-subset}
someGrids <- createPlots(
  project,
  plotGrids = "individual_diagnostics",
  scenarioResults = scenarioResults
)
```

To draw a single Plot on its own, without a grid, pass its id to `plots`. The result is named by the plot's id, and the entry is a single `ggplot` object rather than a `patchwork` grid.

```{r create-plots-single}
single <- createPlots(
  project,
  plots = "p1",
  scenarioResults = scenarioResults
)

single$p1
```

You can ask for grids and single plots in the same call. The result then holds both.

```{r create-plots-both}
both <- createPlots(
  project,
  plotGrids = "individual_diagnostics",
  plots = "p1",
  scenarioResults = scenarioResults
)

names(both)
```

## Observed data

Comparing simulated curves against measurements is what makes a diagnostic figure useful. A project declares its observed data and loads the data when a figure needs it. `vignette("how-to-use-observed-data")` shows how observed data enters a project: the four source types, the source definitions, and `loadObservedData()`. For plotting, you need one name: the **DataSet name** that a DataCombined uses. `getObservedDataNames()` lists the names of all `DataSet` that are available in the project.

```{r observed}
getObservedDataNames(project)
```

Copy the name from `getObservedDataNames()` rather than typing it by hand: it is long and easy to mistype. The predefined `aciclovir_individual` DataCombined already pairs the simulated curve with it, which is why the figure above shows the measurements on top of the prediction. Use the same name when you write your own DataCombined.

## Create your own figures

Beyond a project's predefined figures, you can create new ones in R with `addDataCombined()`, `addPlot()`, and `addPlotGrid()`. Like every other `add*` function, these change the project in your R session only. `saveProject()` writes the changes to the project files, one file per definition in the `definitions/data-combined/`, `definitions/plots/`, and `definitions/plot-grids/` folders.

A new figure takes three steps: a DataCombined collects the curves, a Plot draws them, and a Plot Grid arranges the Plots into a figure.

### Add simulation results to a DataCombined

Read [Working with DataCombined](https://www.open-systems-pharmacology.org/OSPSuite-R/articles/data-combined.html) for details on the `DataCombined` concept.

A simulated curve in a DataCombined names a `scenario` and a `path`: the scenario whose results to draw, and the model output to draw from them. `path` takes either of two forms:

- the full model path in OSPS notation, such as `"Organism|PeripheralVenousBlood|Aciclovir|Plasma (Peripheral Venous Blood)"`
- the id of an Output Path definition, such as `"aciclovir_pvb"`

Output Path definitions are the project's list of named model outputs. They are stored in the `definitions/output-paths/` folder, one file per id, and you add one with `addOutputPath()` (see `vignette("how-to-design-scenarios")`). Print them to see which ids you can use, and pick out one by its id to see the full path behind it:

```{r output-paths}
project$definitions$outputPaths
project$definitions$outputPaths[["aciclovir_pvb"]]
```

Either form draws the same curve. The scenario must record that output, so check that the output path is among the scenario's `outputPaths`.

`label` is optional on a simulated curve. Leave it out and the curve is named by what you wrote in `path`. Write the output-path id there to get a short legend entry:

```{r add-datacombined-short}
addDataCombined(
  project,
  id = "aciclovir_short",
  simulated = list(list(
    scenario = "aciclovir_iv",
    path = "Aciclovir_PVB"
  ))
)
```

Case does not matter in an output-path id: `Aciclovir_PVB` finds the output path `aciclovir_pvb`, and the legend shows `Aciclovir_PVB` as you wrote it. A `path` that names no output-path id is read as a full model path, so a mistyped id is not reported as an unknown id.

### Add observed data to a DataCombined

A DataCombined can also hold observed data, listed under `observed`. Each observed curve names its DataSet by the DataSet name from `getObservedDataNames()` (see [Observed data](#observed-data)). The DataCombined below pairs the simulated peripheral venous blood curve, written here with its full path, with the observed data. Give both curves the same `group`.

```{r add-datacombined}
observedName <- getObservedDataNames(project)[1]

addDataCombined(
  project,
  id = "aciclovir_report",
  simulated = list(list(
    label = "Aciclovir simulated",
    scenario = "aciclovir_iv",
    path = "Organism|PeripheralVenousBlood|Aciclovir|Plasma (Peripheral Venous Blood)",
    group = "Aciclovir PVB"
  )),
  observed = list(list(
    label = "Aciclovir observed",
    dataSet = observedName,
    group = "Aciclovir PVB"
  ))
)
```

Curves with the same `group` share one color and one legend entry. In the figures above, the colored legend entry `Aciclovir PVB` is the group, and the black entries are the curve labels. The group matters most for the observed-versus-simulated and residual plots: they compare a simulated curve only with the observed data in the same group. Without a group, those plots have nothing to compare, and `createPlots()` leaves them out of its result with a warning.

An observed curve always needs a `label`, because DataSet names are long and make poor legend entries. Give every curve in one DataCombined its own label. A simulated curve without `label` is labeled by its `path`, so two such curves with the same `path`, for example the same output from two scenarios, clash. `addDataCombined()` stops on a repeated label and adds nothing.

### Choose a plot type

Next, describe a Plot that draws from this DataCombined. `plotType` selects the kind of chart, see [Plotting with `{ospsuite.plots}`](https://www.open-systems-pharmacology.org/OSPSuite-R/articles/plotting-with-ospsuite-plots.html) for details in the different plot types.

- `individual`: a time profile.
- `population`: a time profile with a band you choose, for a population scenario.
- `observedVsSimulated`: observed values against simulated values.
- `residualsVsSimulated`: residuals against simulated values.
- `residualsVsTime`: residuals against time.

Pass any plot setting through `...`, for example a `title`, an axis unit, axis limits, or a line color. `vignette("reference-definition-fields")` lists every setting and the plot types it applies to.

```{r add-plot}
addPlot(
  project,
  id = "aciclovir_profile",
  dataCombined = "aciclovir_report",
  plotType = "individual",
  title = "Aciclovir IV, individual profile",
  xUnit = "h"
)
```

The same DataCombined can be used for plots of other types. Here an observed-versus-simulated plot, with fold lines at 2-fold around the line of identity, and a plot of the residuals over time:

```{r add-plot-diagnostics}
addPlot(
  project,
  id = "aciclovir_obs_vs_sim",
  dataCombined = "aciclovir_report",
  plotType = "observedVsSimulated",
  title = "Observed vs. simulated",
  foldDistance = 2
)

addPlot(
  project,
  id = "aciclovir_residuals",
  dataCombined = "aciclovir_report",
  plotType = "residualsVsTime",
  title = "Residuals over time",
  xUnit = "h"
)
```

Both compare the simulated curve with the observed data of the same `group`, which is why `aciclovir_report` gives both curves the group `Aciclovir PVB`.

### Arrange plots in a Plot Grid

Finally, add the Plots to a Plot Grid. A grid can hold one plot or several; list every plot id you want in the figure, in the order they should appear.

```{r add-grid}
addPlotGrid(
  project,
  id = "report_figure",
  plots = c("aciclovir_profile", "aciclovir_obs_vs_sim", "aciclovir_residuals"),
  title = "Aciclovir report figure"
)
```

Create the figure using the grid:

```{r build-authored}
reportGrids <- createPlots(
  project,
  plotGrids = "report_figure",
  scenarioResults = scenarioResults
)

reportGrids$report_figure
```

Save the project to write the new definitions to the project files:

```{r save}
saveProject(project)

list.files(file.path(project_dir, "definitions", "plots"))
```

## Plot a population with percentile bands

A population scenario is drawn as a band across the virtual individuals with either time-profile type. Use `plotType = "population"` to choose the band: which percentiles, or a mean with standard deviations. The results of the population scenario `aciclovir_iv_population` are already in `scenarioResults`.

The DataCombined is written exactly as for an individual scenario: name the population scenario and the output path.

```{r population-datacombined}
addDataCombined(
  project,
  id = "aciclovir_population",
  simulated = list(list(
    label = "Aciclovir population",
    scenario = "aciclovir_iv_population",
    path = "Organism|PeripheralVenousBlood|Aciclovir|Plasma (Peripheral Venous Blood)"
  ))
)
```

`quantiles` chooses which percentiles are drawn. It takes fractions, not percentages, so the usual 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles are `c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)`.

```{r population-plot}
addPlot(
  project,
  id = "aciclovir_population_range",
  dataCombined = "aciclovir_population",
  plotType = "population",
  quantiles = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95),
  title = "Aciclovir IV, 5th / 50th / 95th percentile",
  xUnit = "h",
  yAxisScale = "log"
)

populationPlots <- createPlots(
  project,
  plots = "aciclovir_population_range",
  scenarioResults = scenarioResults
)

populationPlots$aciclovir_population_range
```

To show a different range, change the fractions: `quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)` draws the interquartile range. Pass exactly three fractions: lower edge, middle line, upper edge.

Three fields apply only to `plotType = "population"`:

| Field | Controls |
| --- | --- |
| `quantiles` | Which percentiles are drawn, as three fractions. Default: the 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles. Ignored if `aggregation` is not `quantiles` |
| `aggregation` | How the individual curves are summarized: `"quantiles"` (the default), `"arithmetic"` (mean and standard deviation), or `"geometric"` (geometric mean and geometric standard deviation). |
| `nsd` | How many standard deviations the band spans, with `aggregation` set to `"arithmetic"` or `"geometric"`. Default: 1. Ignored when `aggregation = "quantiles"`. |

## Customize the plots

`createPlots()` draws every plot in the ESQlabs house style: text sizes, line and point sizes, the legend at the top left, and the ESQlabs colors. The figures above have it by default. The house values are those of `createEsqlabsPlotConfiguration()`, and every setting you leave out of a Plot takes them.

To change the look of one plot, provide the different properties as arguments to `addPlot`. Here the curve and its observed points are drawn in dark red, the legend goes inside the panel, and the title is bold:

```{r styled-plot}
addPlot(
  project,
  id = "aciclovir_styled",
  dataCombined = "aciclovir_report",
  plotType = "individual",
  title = "Aciclovir IV, individual profile",
  titleFontFace = "bold",
  linesColor = "darkred",
  linesSize = 1,
  legendPosition = "insideTopRight",
  xUnit = "h"
)

styledPlots <- createPlots(
  project,
  plots = "aciclovir_styled",
  scenarioResults = scenarioResults
)

styledPlots$aciclovir_styled
```

## Export a finished figure

Save a figure with `ospsuite.plots::exportPlot()`. It writes one Plot or Plot Grid to a file, by default as a PNG image 16 cm wide at 300 dpi. When you do not give a `height`, it is calculated from the figure, so the panels keep their proportions and the text stays the same size in every figure you export. A legend above or below the panels that needs more room than that makes the figure wider: the report figure below, with its three legends in one row, comes out about 24 cm wide.

The usual place for figures is the `Figures` folder in the project's results folder. `exportPlot()` creates the folder if it does not exist yet.

```{r export-plot}
figuresFolder <- file.path(project$paths$outputFolder, "Figures")

ospsuite.plots::exportPlot(
  reportGrids$report_figure,
  filepath = figuresFolder,
  filename = "aciclovir_report"
)

list.files(figuresFolder)
```

- **`filename` is given without an extension.** `exportPlot()` adds the extension of the file format, and replaces any extension you type: `"aciclovir_report.pdf"` still writes a PNG file.
- **The format is set by `device`**: `"png"` (the default), `"pdf"`, `"svg"`, `"jpeg"`, `"tiff"`, or `"eps"`.
- **The size is set by `width` and `height`**, in centimeters. With `width` alone, a wide legend can still make the figure wider; give both to fix the size exactly.
- **Characters a file name cannot hold**, such as `/`, `:`, or `|`, are replaced by `_`, and `µ` by `u`. `exportPlot()` warns when it changes a name.

Here the same figure is written as a PDF, 24 cm wide and 18 cm high:

```{r export-plot-pdf}
ospsuite.plots::exportPlot(
  reportGrids$report_figure,
  filepath = figuresFolder,
  filename = "aciclovir_report",
  device = "pdf",
  width = 24,
  height = 18
)
```

To change the defaults for every export in your R session, set them once with `ospsuite.plots::setOspsuite.plots.option()`, for example `ospsuite.plots::setOspsuite.plots.option("exportDevice", "pdf")`. The options are `exportWidth`, `exportUnits`, `exportDevice`, and `exportDpi`.

To export several figures, loop over the list that `createPlots()` returns and write each one to its own file, named after the Plot Grid or Plot:

```{r export-plot-loop}
for (name in names(plotGrids)) {
  ospsuite.plots::exportPlot(
    plotGrids[[name]],
    filepath = figuresFolder,
    filename = name
  )
}

list.files(figuresFolder)
```

## Work with a DataCombined in R

To draw a figure, `createPlots()` turns each DataCombined definition into a `DataCombined` object, the object the `{ospsuite}` chart functions draw from. `createDataCombined()` gives you those objects directly. Use it when you need the numbers behind a figure, or a chart that no `plotType` draws.

### Create a DataCombined from its definition

`createDataCombined()` takes the project, the ids of the DataCombined definitions to build, and the scenario results. It returns a list named by id. Instead of `DataCombined` ids, you can pass `plotGrids` to build every DataCombined that the named Plot Grids draw from.

```{r create-datacombined}
dataCombinedList <- createDataCombined(
  project,
  dataCombined = "aciclovir_report",
  scenarioResults = scenarioResults
)
names(dataCombinedList)

dataCombined <- dataCombinedList$aciclovir_report
```

The DataCombined is filled the same way as for a figure: the simulated curves come from `scenarioResults`, the observed data from the project's observed-data sources, and the curve labels, groups, offsets, and scale factors from the definition. `$toDataFrame()` returns every point of every curve as a table, one row per point:

```{r datacombined-table}
curveTable <- dataCombined$toDataFrame()
head(curveTable[, c(
  "name",
  "group",
  "dataType",
  "xValues",
  "xUnit",
  "yValues",
  "yUnit"
)])
```

Each curve keeps its own units in this table: here the simulated curve is in minutes and µmol/l, and the observed data in hours and mg/l.

### Calculate residuals without a plot

`calculateResiduals()` pairs every observed point with the simulated value at the same time, within each group that holds both, and returns the residuals as a table. Use it when you need the residuals as numbers, for example for a goodness-of-fit summary or a table in a report, rather than as a chart. `scaling` sets how a residual is calculated:

- `"log"`: log(simulated) minus log(observed), the residuals the residual plots above draw.
- `"linear"`: simulated minus observed, in the unit of the observed data.
- `"ratio"`: observed divided by simulated.

```{r residuals}
residuals <- calculateResiduals(dataCombined, scaling = "log")
head(residuals[, c(
  "group",
  "xValues",
  "yValuesObserved",
  "yValuesSimulated",
  "residualValues"
)])

# Mean absolute log residual
mean(abs(residuals$residualValues))
```

Here the times and values come in hours and mg/l, the units of the observed data. Pass `xUnit` and `yUnit` to choose the units.

### Draw a chart that has no plot type

Every `{ospsuite}` chart function takes a DataCombined, including the ones no `plotType` covers. `plotResidualsAsHistogram()`, for example, draws the distribution of the residuals. The result is an ordinary `ggplot` object, like everything `createPlots()` returns, so the two can share one figure. Put them side by side with `patchwork::wrap_plots()`:

```{r compose}
residualHistogram <- plotResidualsAsHistogram(dataCombined)

patchwork::wrap_plots(single$p1, residualHistogram)
```

The chart takes the `{ospsuite}` style, not the ESQlabs house style. "Where to go next" below lists more chart types without a `plotType`.

### Build a DataCombined by hand

For a one-off comparison that you do not want to keep in the project, create an empty DataCombined with `DataCombined$new()` and fill it yourself. `$addSimulationResults()` takes the simulation results of a scenario, found in `scenarioResults` under the scenario's id, and `$addDataSets()` takes observed data, which `loadObservedData()` loads from the project as a list named by DataSet name. As in a definition, give the simulated and the observed curve the same group to compare them:

```{r datacombined-by-hand}
handMade <- DataCombined$new()

handMade$addSimulationResults(
  scenarioResults$aciclovir_iv$results,
  quantitiesOrPaths = "Organism|PeripheralVenousBlood|Aciclovir|Plasma (Peripheral Venous Blood)",
  names = "Aciclovir simulated",
  groups = "Aciclovir PVB"
)

observedData <- loadObservedData(project)
handMade$addDataSets(
  observedData[[observedName]],
  names = "Aciclovir observed",
  groups = "Aciclovir PVB"
)

plotTimeProfile(handMade, xUnit = "h")
```

A DataCombined built this way exists only in your R session: `saveProject()` does not store it, and `createPlots()` cannot draw it. For a figure you want to keep and build again, write a DataCombined definition with `addDataCombined()` instead.

## Where to go next

The charts above are drawn by the `{ospsuite}` plot functions, which are built on [`{ospsuite.plots}`](https://www.open-systems-pharmacology.org/OSPSuite.Plots/). Three `{ospsuite}` articles cover those charts and how to change them: [Working with `DataCombined` class](https://www.open-systems-pharmacology.org/OSPSuite-R/articles/data-combined.html), [Visualizations with `DataCombined`](https://www.open-systems-pharmacology.org/OSPSuite-R/articles/data-combined-plotting.html), and [Plotting with ospsuite.plots](https://www.open-systems-pharmacology.org/OSPSuite-R/articles/plotting-with-ospsuite-plots.html).

Some chart types have no `plotType`. Look for them before you build a chart by hand:

- `{ospsuite}`: `plotResidualsAsHistogram()` and `plotQuantileQuantilePlot()`.
- `{ospsuite.plots}`: `plotBoxWhisker()`, `plotHistogram()`, `plotQQ()`, `plotRatioVsCov()`, `plotRangeDistribution()`, and `plotForest()`.

For loading the measurements these figures compare against, see `vignette("how-to-use-observed-data")`. For building and running the scenarios that feed them, see `vignette("how-to-design-scenarios")` and `vignette("how-to-run-simulations")`.

For the plot types and every configuration field, see `vignette("reference-definition-fields")`. For why a figure takes three definitions and why `createPlots()` returns Plot Grids, see `vignette("about-the-plotting-model")`.
